slides.title: Exploring the graph of _y_ = _x_^2
slides.lede: A quadratic function with a U-shaped curve.

keyIdea.title: Key idea
keyIdea.body: Opposite _x_-values give the same _y_-value: if _x_ = _a_, then _x_ = −_a_ gives the same _y_.

concepts.body: The graph of _y_ = _x_^2 is a parabola. It opens upwards, because squaring any number gives a result that is zero or positive.
The vertex is at (0, 0). It is the minimum point: no value of _x_ gives a _y_-value below zero.
The curve is symmetrical about the _y_-axis, the line _x_ = 0. Each side is a mirror image of the other.
Every _y_-value satisfies _y_ ≥ 0, and opposite _x_-values give the same _y_-value: (−3)^2 and 3^2 are both 9.
The curve is flat near the vertex and rises more steeply as _x_ moves away from 0, because the gap between consecutive squares grows.

items.body: three left of the axis, nine up
three right of the axis, nine up

slides.title: Worked examples
slides.lede: Three problems on _y_ = _x_^2, each worked through in full.

examples.label: Example 1
examples.question: Use the rule _y_ = _x_^2 to find _y_ when _x_ = −4.

steps.text: Substitute the given value of _x_. Keep the brackets — the whole of −4 is squared, not just the 4.
Evaluate. A negative multiplied by a negative gives a positive.

examples.label: Example 2
examples.question: Find the value(s) of _x_ for which _y_ = 16.

steps.text: Substitute the known _y_-value into the rule.
Take the square root of both sides. A positive number has two square roots, so both signs must be kept.
Read the answer off the graph as a check: the horizontal line _y_ = 16 crosses the parabola twice, once on each side of the axis of symmetry.
steps.note: This is why a quadratic equation usually has two solutions rather than one.

examples.label: Example 3
examples.question: The point (3, 9) lies on the graph of _y_ = _x_^2. Use symmetry to name another point with the same _y_-value, and explain why it must be there.

steps.text: Identify the axis of symmetry. For _y_ = _x_^2 it is the _y_-axis, the line _x_ = 0.
Measure the horizontal distance from the axis to the given point.
Reflect that distance to the other side of the axis.
Confirm with the rule rather than by eye.
State the reason: squaring removes the sign, so _x_ and −_x_ always give the same _y_.
steps.note: Every point on the curve except the vertex has exactly one partner.

examples.result: (−3, 9). It is the mirror image of (3, 9) in the _y_-axis.

watchFor.title: Watch for
items: How the table of values connects to the graph.

How symmetry makes opposite _x_-values give the same _y_-value.
